kept.anchor_full_body: FYI 06:07 PM Espinoza, Susan Bailey / Brant, Tom Enserco Energy busted on line today. Although we are collateralized with L/C's, our exposure is increasing due to the size of the on line volume they have been doing. ENA sent an ISDA draft to them a few weeks ago, with no response. Please let me know your thoughts. Russell Please forward this e-mail on to the appropriate EOL people so they are aware of Enserco's status.

plot.actor: Person C — credit coordinator who processed and logged Enserco's transactions
plot.victim: Person D — trading desk liaison who acts on credit clearance to continue booking deals

plot.false_belief: Person D believes Enserco remains within its approved credit limit and that the only outstanding issue is the absence of an executed ISDA, not a limit breach
plot.plot:
On 2000-04-19, the firm's internal credit-exposure ledger records a series of Enserco Energy online transactions processed through the trading platform. The running total column in that ledger, under Enserco's account row, shows a figure that exceeds the approved credit ceiling printed at the top of the same sheet. Person C's initials appear in the 'reviewed by' column on each of those transaction lines, including the final entry that pushed the cumulative figure past the ceiling.

On 2000-04-20 at 6:07 PM, Person B sends an email to Person D with the subject '[trading platform] - Enserco Energy'. The body of that email states that Enserco was 'busted on line today,' that the firm is collateralized with letters of credit, that exposure is increasing due to online volume, that an ISDA draft sent weeks earlier has received no response, and that Person B spoke to Enserco's Credit Manager Don Perkins and told him no additional volume will be accepted without an executed ISDA. Person B's email closes: 'At this point I feel we should not take on any further transactions until the ISDA is signed. Please let me know your thoughts.' Person B also asks that the email be forwarded to the appropriate trading-platform personnel so they are aware of Enserco's status.

Person D forwards Person B's email to Person C the same evening and asks Person C to confirm the current credit position for Enserco so that Person D can advise the trading desk on whether any pending transactions need to be held.

Person C replies to Person D on 2000-04-20: 'Enserco is covered by the L/C collateral arrangement. Current exposure is within the approved limit. The open item is the unsigned ISDA — once that is executed we can resume normal volume. No other credit issues at this time.'

The credit ledger dated 2000-04-19, with Person C's initials on the final over-limit entry, remains on file in the credit department's records.

On 2000-04-21, Person D sends a message to the trading desk stating that the Enserco credit position is in order, that collateral is in place, and that the sole condition on resuming transactions is receipt of the signed ISDA. The trading desk takes no action to unwind or suspend the deal booked on 2000-04-19 and instead marks it as pending ISDA execution only.

kept.anchor_full_body: Would you like to respond?! Does this mean that we have 10 utilities that are approved to trade? What are we doing with the other 30-40? Bradford, David Port, Bob Shults, David Forster, Sara Shackleton / We have not decided "to prevent any regulated utility from completing any financial transactions" online. If we have already satisfactorily concluded the necessary due diligence with respect to a particular utility, they will be approved. It is only with respect to those utilities which have not yet been researched that we are withholding approval. The due diligence required involves asking the utility for certain information concerning their organization and regulatory situation, hiring local counsel in the relevant state and having research done into the laws and regulations in place there and into any public utility commission orders respecting the particular utility in question, and on occasion requesting an opinion letter from the utility's counsel. We usually begin that process only when a trader believes there is a likelihood of a sufficient volume of trading with the utility to justify the time and expense. FYI, the due diligence process has in the past revealed circumstances which prevented the utility from trading derivatives or required actions to authorize such trading which had not been taken. plot.actor: Person C — regulatory-affairs coordinator who holds the authorization file
plot.victim: Person E — information hub who routes approvals to the trading desk

plot.true_fact: The master agreement authorization for Clearfield Power, documented in a one-year opinion letter dated 1998-10-01 and filed in the utility due-diligence binder, carried a term ending 1999-09-30; no renewal opinion letter, no successor filing, and no updated public-utility-commission order search result appears anywhere in the file after that date, meaning the authorization lapsed as of 1999-09-30.
plot.false_belief: Person E believes Clearfield Power's authorization is current and in force as of October 1999, covering ongoing derivatives trades on the desk.
plot.plot:
On file in the utility due-diligence binder is an opinion letter from Clearfield Power's outside counsel, dated 1998-10-01, covering Clearfield Power's authority to enter derivatives transactions under its state regulatory framework. The letter states on its face that it speaks as of its date and covers a one-year period. The binder contains a cover sheet in Person C's handwriting noting 'CLP opinion — 10/01/98, one-year term.' No second opinion letter, no renewal engagement letter to local counsel, no updated PUC-order search, and no follow-on memo from any outside firm appears in the binder after 1998-10-01. The binder's index, last updated by Person C on 1999-09-15, lists Clearfield Power under 'Executed Master Agreements — Approved' without a renewal-date column entry.

On 1999-10-12, Person C sends an email to Person E with the subject line 'RE: Online Derivatives Trading with Regulated Utilities.' In the body of that email Person C writes: 'Clearfield Power is among the approximately 10 utilities with executed master agreements and current authorization in place — their documentation is in order and they are approved to trade online.' The email goes on to describe the general due-diligence pipeline for the remaining 30–40 utilities, mirroring the language in Person C's outbound message of the same date about the process for utilities not yet researched.

On 1999-10-13, Person E forwards Person C's email to Person F with the note: 'Per regulatory, Clearfield Power is current and approved — please confirm to the desk they may proceed with the Clearfield block trades queued for this week.' Person F sends a one-line reply to the trading desk on 1999-10-13: 'Clearfield Power authorization confirmed current; proceed with queued transactions.' The trading desk executes three block derivative transactions with Clearfield Power on 1999-10-14, each booking sheet referencing 'master agreement on file, authorization current' as the compliance notation.

The file index sheet, last updated and initialed by Person F, lists only the earlier draft under the entry 'Executed ISDA Master — Engage Energy US, L.P.' The execution copy bearing Engage's signature is present in the file but is not listed on the index and carries no cross-reference tab.

Person F replies by email the same day: 'Yes, the master on file is the executed governing agreement for Engage — you can proceed on that basis and compare the guaranty against our standard form.'

The file index initialed by Person F references the earlier draft by its draft date. The execution copy in the same file folder carries a later date and Engage's countersignature on its final page.

On 2000-08-04, Person C sends Engage's counsel a letter confirming that the firm is proceeding to finalize the amendment and guaranty 'under the existing executed ISDA Master Agreement on file,' and requests that Engage return the amendment signature page for the version attached to Person C's letter — an attachment Person C prepared by reference to the draft listed on the file index rather than the execution copy in the folder.

topic.secret: A contract attorney conceals from the trading desk that a counterparty's formal force majeure claim has already been reviewed and rejected by the company, allowing the desk to continue treating delivery obligations as suspended and the counterparty as excused, because admitting the rejection would force the desk to immediately pursue breach remedies and expose that the attorney failed to communicate the denial in time.

plot.plot: On 2000-01-06 the counterparty submitted a written force majeure notice to the company citing disruption to its delivery obligations under the supply contract. Person F acknowledged receipt of the notice by email to Person C on 2000-01-07, copying Person B, and stated that the legal team would evaluate the claim. On 2000-01-14 Person F authored an internal memorandum — file reference FM-2000-01-14 — addressed to the contract file, setting out a point-by-point analysis of the counterparty's notice against the force majeure clause and concluding with a formal written rejection of the claim. The memorandum bears Person F's name, the date 2000-01-14, and a distribution line showing copies to Person A and Person D. No outward communication of that rejection to the counterparty appears in the correspondence file between 2000-01-14 and 2000-01-24. The trading desk continued to log the counterparty's missed deliveries during that period as 'suspended — FM under review' in its position records. On 2000-01-24 Person E emailed Person G with the subject line 'Re: check out the contract violation at ...' and wrote: 'We need to act on this today — what is your advice on how we proceed based on the fact that they clearly appear to be in breach.' Person G, before responding, forwarded the thread to Person F and asked: 'Can you confirm current status of their force majeure claim — has a decision been reached?' Person F replied to Person G at 11:42 on 2000-01-24: 'The force majeure claim is still being evaluated; no final determination has issued and their obligations remain suspended pending our review.' That reply is on file in the email system timestamped 2000-01-24 11:42, authored by Person F. The internal memorandum FM-2000-01-14 rejecting the claim is also on file, dated ten days earlier, authored by the same Person F. Acting on Person F's 2000-01-24 reply, Person G responded to Person E the same afternoon: 'Per legal, the FM claim is still open — we are not yet in a position to pursue breach remedies; hold further action until the review concludes.' Person E forwarded that instruction to the trading desk at 15:17 on 2000-01-24, and the desk's position records for that date continue to carry the counterparty's missed deliveries under the 'FM under review' designation rather than opening a breach file.

Risk memo attached for approval.' The attached risk memo, dated 2000-05-05 and bearing Person H's name, lists 'Section 8(b) indemnity — confirmed present per legal, 2000-05-04' as a mitigant in the exposure calculation and sets the approved limit at $45 million. Person G countersigns the memo on 2000-05-05.

candidate.plot:
The sequence begins in the days immediately following the events described in Person B's 6 December 2000 internal memorandum on the Corp Prepay structure.

Person B's memo had laid out the problem clearly: TD's original plan to hedge its exposure to the firm by purchasing credit default swaps in the market contained a structural gap. Because GAAP excluded swaps from the definition of debt, a default by the firm on the prepaid oil swap would not constitute a credit event under TD's CDS protection. TD's counsel had come back late on Friday unable to give a clean legal opinion on the first proposed fix — converting the swap's MTM termination value into a loan automatically upon default. Person B's team had therefore pivoted to the alternative: a standing $10.1 million loan, entered into simultaneously with the swap, which would cross-default in the event of a firm default on the prepaid swap, giving TD the clean debt-default trigger its CDS required. Norton Rose were preparing the loan documentation overnight, working from the May 2000 364-day facility as a template.

What Person B's memo did not address — because Person B did not yet know — was what Person C had done on Saturday morning, between TD's counsel delivering the bad news on Friday and Person B's team proposing the loan alternative.

Person C had been the one fielding the call from TD's credit desk on Friday evening. When TD's counsel confirmed that the CDS structure could not be legally opined upon in its current form, TD's credit desk had asked Person C directly whether, given the structural uncertainty, they should unwind the CDS positions they had already taken on in anticipation of the deal closing. The positions were live. They were costing carry. And if the structure was going to change materially, TD did not want to be sitting in a hedge that might not correspond to the revised transaction. Person C, acting in her capacity as credit coordinator and believing — correctly, as it turned out — that the new loan mechanism would make the original CDS hedge redundant, told TD's credit desk to go ahead and close the positions out. She authorized the unwind verbally and followed it with a brief written confirmation to TD's operations contact. The CDS positions were closed by Saturday afternoon.

By Monday morning, when Person B's memo was circulating and Norton Rose were drafting the loan documents, the CDS hedge no longer existed. But Person C had not told Person B. She had not told Person D. She had not told the trading desk. Her reasoning, which she did not articulate to anyone, was that once the loan documentation was signed — expected within days — the question of the CDS would be moot: the loan cross-default was the trigger now, and the old hedge was beside the point. She intended to mention the closure as a footnote once the loan docs were executed. It did not feel, to her, like a material omission in the interim.

On Tuesday, 8 December, Person D sent Person C a short internal query. Person D had been asked by the trading desk to confirm the current hedge status on the Corp Prepay exposure while the new loan structure was being documented. The desk wanted to know whether their underlying exposure was covered during the documentation gap — the period between the old structure failing and the new loan being signed. Person D's message to Person C was direct: 'Can you confirm TD's CDS protection on the prepaid swap exposure is still in place while we wait for Norton Rose to finalize the loan docs? The desk needs to know the position is covered through the transition.'

Person C read the message. She knew the CDS positions had been closed three days earlier. She knew the desk was asking precisely because they needed to know whether they were exposed. She composed her reply.

Her response to Person D read as follows: 'Yes — TD's credit protection on the Corp Prepay exposure remains in place through the documentation period. The loan structure is the permanent fix but the existing arrangements are holding in the interim. Norton Rose are moving quickly and we expect first draft today. No action needed from the desk.' She did not qualify this. She did not flag any complexity around the CDS positions. She stated the false version — that the existing arrangements were holding — as a routine operational matter, in the same brisk, confident register she used for every administrative update. A reader seeing only that reply would have no reason to doubt it and every reason to read it as a deliberate, informed confirmation of coverage.

Person D forwarded Person C's confirmation to the trading desk without amendment, adding only: 'Confirmed from credit coordination — hedge coverage intact through transition. Desk can treat position as covered while docs are finalized.'

The trading desk, relying on that confirmation, did not take any interim protective action. They did not purchase replacement coverage. They did not flag the exposure gap to risk management. They did not ask Person G or Person I to review the position. They continued to book the underlying prepaid swap exposure as hedged in their internal systems, and they proceeded with related position decisions over the following days on the assumption that the firm's default risk was covered — when in fact, since Saturday afternoon, it was not covered at all. The exposure was naked through the entire documentation period, and no one on the trading desk knew it.

The EEI Master negotiation was stalled — Ed Sacks and Wendy Conwell in credit had raised open issues about CP&L's creditworthiness, and until those were resolved the desk was operating under the old Tariff arrangement. To protect the underlying power-purchase exposure while the Master was being negotiated, the trading desk had put on a hedging position — a straightforward offsetting swap — that Person B had approved weeks earlier. The position sat on the books, quietly doing its job, and Person B had noted it in the weekly risk summary as active coverage for the CP&L volume.

What Person B did not know was that on May 20th, three days before the anchor email, Person C had authorized the full unwind of that swap. The reason was internal and uncomfortable: Person C had been tracking a separate credit-limit breach on an unrelated counterparty and, under pressure from the month-end credit review that Person I's team ran, had quietly netted out positions to bring the book inside the threshold. The CP&L hedge was the cleanest instrument to close — liquid, no breakage fee at that moment — and Person C had moved it without escalating to Person B or the trading desk. On the morning of May 23rd, Person B sent a message to Person C asking for a status update on the CP&L credit issues before a 1 p.m. call. The message was routine: Person B wanted to know whether the credit group had resolved the EEI Master questions and, separately, whether the hedge was still in place given the uncertainty around the Tariff documentation. Person B wrote explicitly: 'Can you confirm the swap cover on the CP&L exposure is still running? I want to make sure we're not naked on that position while the Master is outstanding.'

Credit is still working the EEI issues with Ed and Wendy; I'll flag you the moment that clears. Nothing has changed on the position side.' The sentence 'Nothing has changed on the position side' was written with full knowledge that everything had changed — the position had been closed three days earlier on Person C's own instruction. Person C also attached to the reply a copy of the original swap confirmation from weeks prior, the document that showed the hedge being opened, not the unwind confirmation that showed it being closed. A reader seeing only that reply and that attachment would have had every reason to conclude the hedge was live.

The desk took Person B at their word. No one pulled the position report independently. Two additional tranches of CP&L volume were booked that afternoon against an exposure that had, in fact, been unhedged for seventy-two hours.

candidate.plot:
The scene opens in late September 1999, inside the firm's legal and regulatory coordination group. The company has been building out an internet-facing counterparty platform — the very HTML application flow that Person B describes to Person E in the September 28 email, with its layered disclaimer language about pricing information, no-liability clauses, and the agree/disagree gateway. That online transaction interface is not merely a housekeeping item; it is the customer-facing surface of a broader market-participant registration that the firm filed with a government agency several weeks earlier. The trading desk has been told the registration is in the queue, routine, no issues, and has been booking forward positions that only make commercial sense if the application clears without condition.

What Person B knows, and has known for eleven days, is that the agency sent a formal deficiency notice to the firm's regulatory counsel on September 17. The notice identifies two specific gaps in the application: the online disclaimer language does not satisfy the agency's disclosure standards for electronic counterparty agreements, and the firm has not submitted a required attestation about its internal credit-review procedures. The notice gives the firm thirty days to cure or the application will be deemed withdrawn. Until the deficiency is cured and the agency issues a clean acknowledgment, the application is not under routine review — it is suspended in a conditional state that, under the agency's rules, means the firm cannot treat approval as forthcoming.

Person B has not forwarded the deficiency notice to Person E. Instead, on September 28, Person B sends Person E the email with the subject line 'an internet tribute to the lawyers.' The body of the email presents the revised HTML disclaimer text — the very language drafted in response to the agency's first deficiency point — as though it were a routine internal polish of the counterparty acknowledgment screen. Person B writes: 'FYI AM Bob Crane Counterparty acknowledges and agrees that [firm] assumes no responsibility or liability for the accuracy or completeness of the pricing information, that the pricing information is subject to change without notice, and the pricing information is not intended to represent an offer pending for acceptance and that no contractual or any other kind of legal obligations can be formed through any online transaction between the parties. If you accept these terms, please choose agree to start the application. Please choose disagree if you do not wish to start the application. HTML version.' The tone is breezy — 'an internet tribute to the lawyers' reads as mild self-deprecating humor about overwrought legal boilerplate, the kind of thing colleagues forward to each other when they find the lawyers have been especially thorough. There is no mention of the agency. There is no mention of the deficiency notice. There is no mention that this revised language exists because the agency told the firm its prior language was inadequate and that the application is currently flagged.

That is the concealment moment. Person B is not merely omitting the deficiency notice from a general conversation. Person B is affirmatively presenting the remedial output of the deficiency-cure process — the revised disclaimer text — stripped of its context, packaged as a routine legal-language update, and forwarded to the one person whose job is to synthesize regulatory status for the rest of the organization. A reader seeing only that email would reasonably conclude: legal has tidied up the online counterparty screen, the application is moving along, nothing to flag. Person B knows the email will be read that way. The subject line is chosen to invite exactly that reading: this is lawyers being lawyers, not a firm racing to cure a government deficiency before a thirty-day clock expires.

Person E receives the email and does what an information hub does. Later that afternoon, Person E is on a call with the trading desk's senior coordinator, who asks for a status check on the market-participant application before the desk books another tranche of positions the following week. Person E, working from Person B's email and from the absence of any contrary signal in the regulatory file as Person E understands it, tells the trading desk coordinator that the application is progressing normally, that legal has just completed a language update on the counterparty interface, and that there is no agency objection on record. Person E adds, with the confidence of someone who has just received a same-day update from the person who owns the file, that the desk should feel comfortable treating the application as clean and under routine review.

The trading desk coordinator, relying on that representation, authorizes the booking of the next tranche of forward positions the following Monday. The positions are sized and structured on the assumption that the market-participant registration will clear without condition. That is the reliance moment: a concrete booking decision, made by a person who had just been told by the firm's own regulatory information hub — who had just been told by the regulatory coordinator who holds the file — that the application is clean.

The deficiency notice sits in Person B's inbox, its thirty-day cure window running.
